name: Sumerian city-states
capital: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish and others (no single capital)
summary: A patchwork of rival city-states in southern Mesopotamia that produced the earliest known writing, monumental temples and law codes. The Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112–2004 BCE) briefly unified the region before falling to Elam.

sources.cite: Sumerian King List (Weld-Blundell Prism, Ashmolean Museum AN1923.444)
sources.note: Lists kings and cities; early reigns are legendary.
Literary account of Ur's destruction c. 2004 BCE.

sources.cite: Royal Cemetery of Ur, excavated by C. L. Woolley 1922–1934
Proto-cuneiform tablets from the Eanna precinct, Uruk (German excavations from 1912)

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Founded by Sargon of Akkad, often called the first empire: a single dynasty ruling Sumer and northern Mesopotamia and campaigning to the Mediterranean. Dates follow the conventional middle chronology and carry uncertainty of decades.

sources.cite: Royal inscriptions of Sargon and Naram-Sin, Old Babylonian copies from Nippur (ed. Frayne, RIME 2)
Bassetki Statue of Naram-Sin, found 1974 near Duhok, Iraq

name: Ancient Egypt
capital: Memphis, Thebes, Amarna, Tanis and others over time
summary: Unified under the first pharaohs around 3100 BCE, Egypt endured through Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, foreign dynasties and Ptolemaic Greek rule until Rome annexed it in 30 BCE. The New Kingdom under Thutmose III was its widest extent.

sources.cite: Narmer Palette, Hierakonpolis (Egyptian Museum, Cairo JE 32169)
Manetho, Aegyptiaca (3rd c. BCE; fragments via Josephus, Africanus, Eusebius)
sources.note: Source of the dynasty numbering still used today.

sources.cite: Wadi al-Jarf papyri ('Diary of Merer'), found 2013

name: Elam
summary: A long-lived civilization of south-western Iran, perennial rival of the Mesopotamian powers. Elam toppled Ur in 2004 BCE and was itself crushed by Ashurbanipal of Assyria around 646 BCE before being absorbed into Persia.

sources.cite: French excavations at Susa from 1884 (Dieulafoy, de Morgan)

name: Indus Valley Civilization
capital: No known capital; major cities include Mohenjo-daro and Harappa
summary: One of the three earliest urban civilizations, with planned grid cities, drainage and standardized weights across a territory larger than Egypt or Mesopotamia. Its script remains undeciphered, so its history is known only from archaeology.

sources.cite: J. Marshall, Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization (1931)
Harappa excavations, M. S. Vats (1920s–30s); Harappa Archaeological Research Project (from 1986)
Indus seals and script (c. 4,000 inscriptions), undeciphered

name: Minoan Crete
summary: A Bronze Age palace civilization on Crete with far-reaching sea trade. After about 1450 BCE Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos, writing in Linear B instead of the undeciphered Minoan Linear A.

sources.cite: Knossos excavations by Arthur Evans, from 1900
Akrotiri (Thera), excavated by S. Marinatos from 1967

name: Hittite Kingdom
summary: An Anatolian great power that sacked Babylon, fought Egypt at Kadesh and signed the earliest surviving peace treaty. The kingdom collapsed around 1180 BCE; the later 'Hittites' on maps are Neo-Hittite city-states in Syria and southern Anatolia.

sources.cite: Boğazköy (Hattusa) tablet archives, c. 30,000 fragments; language deciphered by B. Hrozný in 1915

sources.note: Narrates the early kings and the sack of Babylon.

sources.cite: Treaty of Kadesh, Hittite version (Istanbul Archaeology Museums)
German excavations at Hattusa from 1906 (Winckler; later Bittel, Neve, Seeher, Schachner)

name: Troy (Wilusa)
summary: A fortified city at the mouth of the Dardanelles occupied in successive layers (Troy I–IX). It was probably the Wilusa of Hittite texts, a vassal kingdom. Layer VIIa burned around 1180 BCE; whether that matches Homer's Trojan War is still debated.

sources.cite: Alaksandu Treaty between Muwatalli II and Alaksandu of Wilusa (CTH 76), c. 1280 BCE

name: Greek world
capital: Many city-states: Mycenae, Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Thebes
summary: From the Mycenaean palace kingdoms through the city-states of the classical age, Greek speakers spread colonies from Spain to the Black Sea. Rome's destruction of Corinth in 146 BCE ended Greek independence.

sources.cite: Linear B tablets from Pylos and Knossos (deciphered by M. Ventris, 1952)
Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
Mycenae, Grave Circle A (Schliemann 1876); Athenian Agora excavations (from 1931)

name: Assyria
summary: A northern Mesopotamian state that became the first empire to rule from Egypt to Iran. Its Neo-Assyrian phase relied on mass deportation and royal propaganda carved in stone. Nineveh fell to Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE.

sources.cite: Library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh (found by Layard and Rassam, 1849–1854)
Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace (British Museum)

name: Babylonia
summary: Hammurabi made Babylon the heart of southern Mesopotamia in the 18th century BCE. After centuries under Kassites and Assyrians, the Neo-Babylonian Empire of Nebuchadnezzar II dominated the Near East until Cyrus took the city in 539 BCE.

sources.cite: Code of Hammurabi stele (Louvre Sb 8), found at Susa in 1901
Babylon excavations by R. Koldewey, 1899–1917 (Ishtar Gate, now Berlin)

name: Kingdom of Kush
summary: A Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile whose kings conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty. Driven back south by Assyria, Kush flourished at Meroë, building more pyramids than Egypt, until its decline in the 4th century CE.

sources.cite: Victory Stela of Piye, Gebel Barkal (Egyptian Museum, Cairo JE 48862)

sources.note: Records an Aksumite campaign against Kush.

sources.cite: Meroë pyramids; G. A. Reisner's excavations (1916–1923)

name: Olmec
summary: The earliest known major civilization of Mesoamerica, on the Gulf Coast of Mexico. It is known for its colossal basalt heads and for influences in art and ritual that later cultures inherited. It left no deciphered texts.

sources.cite: La Venta excavations by M. Stirling (1940s) and P. Drucker
San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, M. Coe (1966–68) and A. Cyphers (from 1990)

name: Shang dynasty
summary: The first Chinese dynasty attested by its own writing. Oracle bones from Anyang record royal divinations and confirm the king list later given by Sima Qian. The Zhou overthrew it at the Battle of Muye.

sources.cite: Oracle bone inscriptions from Yinxu, Anyang (identified 1899)
Sima Qian, Shiji, ch. 3 'Basic Annals of Yin' (c. 94 BCE)

name: Zhou dynasty
summary: China's longest dynasty. The Western Zhou ruled through kin-based fiefs. After 771 BCE royal power faded and the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods fragmented China until Qin extinguished the last Zhou king.

sources.note: Dates the conquest of Shang to a jiazi day.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji, ch. 4 'Basic Annals of Zhou'
Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals) with the Zuozhuan commentary

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Built by Cyrus the Great and organized into satrapies by Darius I, the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean to the Indus. Alexander of Macedon conquered it between 334 and 330 BCE.

sources.cite: Behistun Inscription of Darius I (Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian), copied by H. Rawlinson 1835–1847
Persepolis Fortification and Treasury tablets (Oriental Institute excavations, 1930s)

name: Carthage
summary: A Phoenician colony from Tyre that became the dominant sea power of the western Mediterranean. Three Punic Wars with Rome ended with the city's destruction in 146 BCE.

sources.cite: Polybius, Histories, books 1–3 and fragments of 36–39
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita, books 21–30 (Second Punic War)
Tophet of Salammbô and the circular naval harbour (UNESCO 'Save Carthage' campaign, 1970s)

name: Rome
capital: Rome; later Milan and Ravenna in the West
summary: From a small kingdom on the Tiber, Rome became a republic and then an empire ruling the whole Mediterranean. It reached its widest extent under Trajan in 117 CE. The western half ended in 476; the eastern half continued as the Byzantine Empire.

sources.cite: Res Gestae Divi Augusti (Monumentum Ancyranum, Ankara)
Pompeii and Herculaneum (excavated from 1738/1748); Vindolanda tablets (from 1973)

name: Empire of Alexander
summary: In thirteen years Alexander III of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire and reached the Indus. When he died at Babylon in 323 BCE his generals split the empire into the Hellenistic kingdoms, including the Seleucid and Ptolemaic states.

sources.cite: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander (2nd c. CE, using Ptolemy and Aristobulus)

sources.note: Records the king's death in Babylon, June 323 BCE.

sources.cite: Royal tombs at Vergina (Aigai), excavated by M. Andronikos 1977

name: Maurya Empire
summary: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya, it united most of the Indian subcontinent. His grandson Ashoka turned to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war and carved his edicts across the empire.

sources.cite: Edicts of Ashoka (rock and pillar inscriptions; Brahmi deciphered by J. Prinsep, 1837)
Megasthenes, Indica (fragments in Arrian, Strabo, Diodorus)
Pataliputra excavations at Kumrahar (D. B. Spooner, 1912–15)

name: Seleucid Empire
capital: Seleucia on the Tigris, then Antioch
summary: The largest successor state of Alexander's empire, founded by Seleucus I and stretching at first from Anatolia to Bactria. Defeat by Rome at Magnesia and the rise of Parthia shrank it to Syria, which Pompey annexed in 63 BCE.

sources.cite: Babylonian Astronomical Diaries and chronicles (British Museum)

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
summary: A Macedonian Greek dynasty ruling Egypt from Alexandria, home of the Library and the Pharos. It ended with Cleopatra VII's death and Octavian's annexation of Egypt in 30 BCE.

sources.cite: Rosetta Stone, Memphis Decree of 196 BCE (British Museum EA 24)
Oxyrhynchus and other Greek papyri from Egypt

name: Qin dynasty
summary: The western state of Qin conquered its Warring States rivals, and its king proclaimed himself First Emperor in 221 BCE. He standardized script, coins and weights. The dynasty collapsed within four years of his death.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji, ch. 6 'Basic Annals of the First Emperor'
Shuihudi Qin bamboo slips (legal texts, found 1975)
Terracotta Army pits near the First Emperor's mausoleum (found 1974)

name: Han dynasty
summary: Founded by Liu Bang, the Han set the model for imperial China: Confucian officialdom, salt and iron monopolies and expansion into Central Asia that opened the Silk Roads. The dynasty ended in 220 CE, splitting China into the Three Kingdoms.

sources.cite: Fan Ye, Hou Hanshu (Book of the Later Han)

name: Parthian Empire
summary: The Arsacid dynasty of Parthia took Iran and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids and held Rome at bay for nearly three centuries, most famously at Carrhae. Its own vassal Ardashir overthrew it in 224 CE.

sources.cite: Old Nisa, Turkmenistan (Soviet and Italian excavations)

name: Germanic peoples
summary: Speakers of Germanic languages north of the Rhine and Danube. Roman writers described them, and they destroyed three legions at the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. Their migrations in the 4th–6th centuries reshaped Europe into the kingdoms of Goths, Franks, Vandals and Anglo-Saxons.

name: Goths
summary: A Germanic people who crossed the Danube, defeated Rome at Adrianople and sacked Rome in 410. They founded the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy, ended by Justinian in 553, and the Visigothic Kingdom in Spain, which fell to the Umayyads in 711.

name: Vandal Kingdom
summary: The Vandals crossed the Rhine in 406, passed through Gaul and Spain, and under Gaiseric seized Roman Africa and Carthage in 439. They sacked Rome in 455. Belisarius destroyed the kingdom for Justinian in 533–534.

sources.cite: Procopius, History of the Wars, books 3–4 (Vandal War)
Victor of Vita, History of the Vandal Persecution (c. 484)
Albertini Tablets (Vandal-era deeds on wood, found 1928)

name: Huns
capital: Royal camp on the Hungarian plain
summary: Steppe horsemen whose arrival north of the Black Sea around 370 pushed the Goths into the Roman Empire. Under Attila they extorted gold from both Roman empires. Their realm broke apart after his death in 453.

sources.cite: Priscus of Panium, fragments (embassy to Attila, 449)

name: Sasanian Empire
summary: The last pre-Islamic Persian empire, Rome's great rival for four centuries. Shapur I captured a Roman emperor in 260. Exhausted by war with Byzantium, it fell to the Arab conquests by 651.

sources.cite: Shapur I's trilingual inscription at the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (ŠKZ), Naqsh-e Rostam
al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings (10th c.)
Taq Kasra, Ctesiphon; rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur

name: Gupta Empire
summary: North India's 'classical age': Sanskrit literature, mathematics (Aryabhata) and temple art flourished under the Guptas. Hunnic invasions and fragmentation ended the empire in the 6th century.

sources.cite: Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta (by Harishena)
Faxian, A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms (travels 399–412)

name: Kingdom of Aksum
summary: A trading power of the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands linking Rome and India through the Red Sea. Under King Ezana in the 4th century it adopted Christianity and conquered Meroë.

sources.cite: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c. CE)
Stelae field of Aksum; Aksumite coinage

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The eastern Roman Empire, which called itself Roman throughout its history and lasted a thousand years after the West fell. Justinian briefly retook Italy and Africa. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

sources.cite: Procopius, Wars, Buildings and Secret History (6th c.)
Kritoboulos and Doukas, accounts of the fall of Constantinople
Hagia Sophia (537); Theodosian Walls; Yenikapı harbour excavations (2004–2013)

name: Maya civilization
capital: Rival city-states: Tikal, Calakmul, Copán, Palenque, later Chichén Itzá and Mayapán
summary: A civilization of competing kingdoms in the Yucatán and Guatemala with the Americas' most complete writing system. The southern lowland cities collapsed in the 9th century. The last independent kingdom, Nojpetén, fell to Spain in 1697.

sources.cite: Classic Maya stelae and inscriptions (decipherment by Knorozov, Proskouriakoff and others from the 1950s)
Tikal Project (University of Pennsylvania, 1956–70); PACUNAM lidar survey (2018)

name: Umayyad Caliphate
summary: The first hereditary caliphate, which carried Arab rule from Iberia to the Indus. It was overthrown by the Abbasid revolution in 750. A surviving prince founded the Emirate (later Caliphate) of Córdoba.

sources.cite: Dome of the Rock dedicatory inscription (AH 72 / 691–92 CE)
al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings

name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: Moving the caliphate east to Baghdad, the Abbasids presided over a golden age of scholarship and trade. From the 10th century real power passed to regional dynasties. The Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last caliph there in 1258.

sources.cite: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings
al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan (on the founding of Baghdad)

name: Tang dynasty
summary: A cosmopolitan dynasty whose capital, Chang'an, was perhaps the world's largest city. Tang power reached into Central Asia until defeat at Talas (751) and the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) weakened it.

sources.cite: Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, 945) and New Book of Tang (Xin Tangshu, 1060)

name: Ghana Empire (Wagadu)
summary: A Soninke kingdom in the western Sahel that grew rich taxing the trans-Saharan gold trade. Arab geographers described its king's court. It declined in the 11th–12th centuries and was succeeded by Mali.

sources.cite: al-Bakri, Book of Routes and Realms (1068)
Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash (17th-c. Timbuktu chronicles)
Koumbi Saleh excavations (from 1914; Thomassey and Mauny, 1949–51)

name: Frankish Kingdom
summary: Clovis united the Franks and converted to Catholic Christianity. The Carolingian Charlemagne ruled most of Western Europe and was crowned emperor in 800. His grandsons divided the realm at Verdun in 843.

sources.cite: Gregory of Tours, Ten Books of Histories (c. 594)

name: Holy Roman Empire
capital: No fixed capital; Vienna under the Habsburgs
summary: A loose elective empire of German, Italian and Bohemian lands claiming the Roman imperial title from Otto I's coronation in 962. It became a federation of princes after the Peace of Westphalia. Francis II dissolved it in 1806 under pressure from Napoleon.

sources.cite: Widukind of Corvey, Deeds of the Saxons (10th c.)
Peace of Westphalia treaties (Osnabrück and Münster, 1648)

name: Kievan Rus'
summary: A federation of East Slavic principalities under the Rurikid dynasty, founded by Varangian (Norse) rulers. It adopted Orthodox Christianity in 988. Fragmentation and the Mongol sack of Kiev in 1240 ended it.

name: Kingdom of England
summary: Æthelstan unified the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in 927. The Normans conquered England in 1066. The kingdom joined Scotland to form Great Britain in 1707.

sources.cite: Domesday Book (1086; The National Archives E 31)
Magna Carta (1215; British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106)

name: Great Britain / United Kingdom
match: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
summary: Formed by the union of England and Scotland, Britain built the largest empire in history, covering roughly a quarter of the world's land around 1920. Most colonies became independent between 1947 and the 1960s.

name: Song dynasty
summary: An era of paper money, movable type, gunpowder weapons and a commercial revolution. The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and fell to Kublai Khan's Mongols in 1279.

sources.cite: Zhang Zeduan, Along the River During the Qingming Festival (scroll, 12th c.)

name: Khmer Empire
summary: A Southeast Asian empire centred on Angkor, a vast city of temples and reservoirs that included Angkor Wat. Jayavarman VII expanded it around 1200. Angkor was abandoned as the capital after Ayutthaya's attack in 1431.

sources.cite: Zhou Daguan, A Record of Cambodia (visit 1296–97)

name: Mongol Empire
summary: Chinggis Khan united the steppe in 1206. His successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary. By 1260 it had split into four khanates. The Yuan dynasty in China fell in 1368.

sources.cite: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th c.)
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles, c. 1307)
William of Rubruck, Itinerarium (visit to Karakorum 1254)

name: Delhi Sultanate
summary: A succession of five Turkic and Afghan dynasties ruling north India from Delhi. It repelled Mongol invasions and briefly reached the far south under Muhammad bin Tughluq. Babur ended it at Panipat in 1526.

name: Mali Empire
summary: Founded by Sundiata Keita, Mali controlled the gold fields and trade cities of the Sahel. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage through Cairo in 1324 made it famous across the Mediterranean world.

sources.cite: Epic of Sundiata (oral tradition of the griots)

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: A Turkish beylik that grew into a three-continent empire. It took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled the Balkans, Middle East and North Africa for centuries. Defeat in the First World War led to the sultanate's abolition in 1922.

sources.cite: Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname (Book of Travels, 17th c.)
Ottoman tax registers (tahrir defterleri), Ottoman Archives, Istanbul

name: Ming dynasty
summary: Founded after the expulsion of the Mongols, the Ming built the Forbidden City and most of the surviving Great Wall, and sent Zheng He's treasure fleets to Africa. Rebels took Beijing in 1644, opening the way for the Manchu Qing.

sources.cite: Ming Shilu (Veritable Records of the Ming)
Liujiagang and Changle inscriptions of Zheng He (1431)

name: Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance)
summary: An alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan that dominated central Mexico through tribute. Spaniards under Cortés, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies and helped by smallpox, captured Tenochtitlan in 1521.

name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
summary: The largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, run without markets or writing through roads, storehouses and knotted-cord khipu records. Civil war and Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 brought its fall.

sources.cite: Juan de Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas (1551)
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (c. 1615)
Machu Picchu (studied by Hiram Bingham, 1911); Qhapaq Ñan road system

name: Songhai Empire
summary: Under Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad, Songhai replaced Mali as the great Sahel power, with Timbuktu as a centre of learning. A Moroccan army with firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591.

name: Safavid Empire
summary: Ismail I founded the Safavid state and made Twelver Shi'ism Iran's official religion, defining modern Iran's identity. Shah Abbas I rebuilt Isfahan as a showpiece capital.

sources.cite: Iskandar Beg Munshi, Tarikh-i Alam-ara-yi Abbasi (1629)

name: Mughal Empire
summary: Babur, a Timurid prince, founded the empire after Panipat. Under Akbar, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb it ruled most of the subcontinent and built the Taj Mahal. British forces deposed the last emperor after the 1857 rebellion.

name: Spanish Empire
summary: United Castile and Aragon launched Columbus's voyages and conquered the Aztec and Inca empires. The resulting empire stretched from California to Tierra del Fuego and the Philippines. Most of the Americas won independence by 1825, and the last overseas colonies were lost in 1898.

sources.cite: Christopher Columbus, log of the first voyage (abstract by Bartolomé de las Casas)
Bartolomé de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552)

name: Qing dynasty
summary: A Manchu dynasty that doubled China's territory by adding Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet. The Qing faltered in the 19th century under the Opium Wars and the Taiping Rebellion. The Xinhai Revolution forced the last emperor to abdicate in 1912.

sources.cite: Edict of abdication of the Xuantong Emperor (12 February 1912)
Qing Grand Council archives, First Historical Archives of China, Beijing

name: Muscovy, Russian Empire and USSR
summary: Muscovy threw off Golden Horde overlordship in 1480 and expanded across Siberia to the Pacific by 1639. Peter I proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. After the 1917 revolutions it was reborn as the Soviet Union, which dissolved in 1991.

sources.cite: Treaty on the Creation of the USSR (30 December 1922)

name: Yamnaya culture
summary: Pontic-Caspian steppe herders who buried their dead under kurgan mounds and used wheeled wagons. Ancient DNA shows a large Yamnaya-related migration into Europe after 3000 BCE, and many scholars link them with early Indo-European languages.

sources.cite: Kurgan burials of the Pontic-Caspian steppe
Haak et al., 'Massive migration from the steppe', Nature (2015)

name: Bell Beaker culture
summary: A pan-European archaeological horizon named after its bell-shaped drinking cups, spreading from Iberia to Britain and Central Europe. In Britain its arrival came with a near-total genetic turnover.

sources.cite: Olalde et al., 'The Beaker phenomenon', Nature (2018)

name: Cycladic culture
summary: Early Bronze Age culture of the Aegean Cyclades, known for its stylized marble figurines and seafaring.

sources.cite: Cycladic figurines; Keros sanctuary excavations (C. Renfrew, from 2006)

name: Norte Chico (Caral)
summary: The oldest known complex society in the Americas: monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas in the valleys of coastal Peru, built without pottery.

name: Kerma
summary: The first great kingdom of Nubia, rival of Middle Kingdom Egypt, with a massive mud-brick temple (the Western Deffufa). Egypt's New Kingdom destroyed it around 1500 BCE.

sources.cite: G. A. Reisner's excavations (1913–16); Charles Bonnet's Swiss mission (from 1977)

name: Oxus civilization (BMAC)
capital: Gonur Depe and other fortified centres
summary: A Bronze Age civilization of fortified oasis towns in today's Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan, trading with Mesopotamia and the Indus.

sources.cite: Gonur Depe excavations by V. Sarianidi (from 1972)

name: Andronovo culture
summary: Bronze Age herders of the Central Asian steppe, linked to the spread of the chariot and of Indo-Iranian languages. Sintashta fortified settlements are its earliest phase.

sources.cite: Sintashta and Arkaim fortified settlements, southern Urals

name: Jōmon culture
summary: Long-lived hunter-gatherer culture of Japan that made some of the world's earliest pottery, named for its cord-marked decoration.

name: Xia (Erlitou)
summary: The first dynasty in Chinese tradition. No Xia writing survives; many archaeologists associate it with the Erlitou culture and its palace complex in Henan.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji, ch. 2 'Basic Annals of Xia'

name: Bantu expansion
summary: Over three millennia, farmers speaking Bantu languages spread from the Nigeria–Cameroon borderland across most of central, eastern and southern Africa, carrying ironworking and agriculture.

sources.cite: Comparative linguistics of the Bantu family
Patin et al., 'Dispersals of Bantu-speaking populations', Science (2017)

name: Mitanni
summary: A Hurrian kingdom of northern Mesopotamia ruled by an Indo-Aryan-named elite, rival of Egypt and the Hittites. Hittite and Assyrian attacks destroyed it.

sources.cite: Amarna letters from Tushratta of Mitanni (EA 17–29)
Treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza (CTH 51)

name: Israel and Judah
summary: Two Iron Age kingdoms of the southern Levant. Assyria destroyed Israel in 720 BCE; Babylon destroyed Judah and Jerusalem's temple in 587 BCE. The Hebrew Bible's history was largely compiled from these traditions.

sources.cite: Tel Dan stele (9th c. BCE), mentioning the 'House of David'

name: Phoenician city-states
summary: Canaanite trading cities of the Lebanese coast that spread the alphabet and founded colonies across the Mediterranean, including Carthage and Cádiz. Alexander's siege of Tyre in 332 BCE ended their independence.

name: Urartu
summary: A highland kingdom around Lake Van, Assyria's northern rival, known for its fortresses and irrigation works.

name: Media
summary: An Iranian kingdom that helped destroy Assyria in 612 BCE and ruled the Iranian plateau until Cyrus the Great absorbed it.

name: Lydia
summary: A western Anatolian kingdom credited with the first coins. Its last king, Croesus, fell to Cyrus in 546 BCE.

name: Scythians
summary: Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the Eurasian steppe, famous for gold animal-style art and rich kurgan burials. Herodotus devoted a whole book to them.

sources.cite: Arzhan and Pazyryk kurgans; Solokha comb (Hermitage)

name: Celtic peoples
capital: Oppida such as Bibracte and Manching
summary: Iron Age peoples of the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures who spread from Central Europe to Iberia, Britain and Anatolia (the Galatians). Rome conquered most of them by the first century CE.

sources.cite: Hallstatt cemetery (from 1846); La Tène site, Lake Neuchâtel

name: Etruscans
capital: Twelve-city league (Veii, Tarquinia, Cerveteri and others)
summary: A non-Indo-European people of central Italy whose culture shaped early Rome. Rome absorbed their cities one by one, ending with Volsinii in 264 BCE.

sources.cite: Painted tombs of Tarquinia; Cerveteri necropolis

name: Saba (Sheba)
summary: A South Arabian kingdom that grew rich on frankincense and myrrh, famous for the Marib Dam. Himyar conquered it around 275 CE.

sources.cite: Marib Dam and Temple of Awwam

name: Nabataean Kingdom
summary: Arab caravan traders who carved Petra from rose-red rock. Trajan annexed the kingdom as the province of Arabia in 106 CE.

name: Himyarite Kingdom
summary: Dominant power of South Arabia in late antiquity whose rulers converted to Judaism. Aksum invaded and ended it around 525 CE.

name: Dacia
summary: A kingdom north of the Danube unified by Burebista and later Decebalus. Trajan conquered it in two wars (101–106 CE), commemorated on his column.

name: Kingdom of Pergamon
summary: A Hellenistic kingdom under the Attalid dynasty, Rome's ally against the Seleucids, famous for its library and the Great Altar. Attalus III bequeathed it to Rome.

name: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
summary: The easternmost Greek state, founded by Diodotus I when he broke from the Seleucids. Its successors ruled in north-west India as the Indo-Greek kingdoms.

name: Xiongnu
capital: Royal court in the Orkhon valley
summary: The first great steppe empire, founded by Modu Chanyu, which forced the early Han dynasty to pay tribute. It split in 48 CE and its southern branch was absorbed into China.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji, ch. 110 'Account of the Xiongnu'
Noin-Ula and Gol Mod elite tombs, Mongolia

name: Kushan Empire
summary: A Central Asian dynasty that ruled from the Oxus to the Ganges at a crossroads of Silk Road trade. Under Kanishka it patronized Buddhism and Gandharan art.

name: Satavahana Empire
summary: A Deccan dynasty that controlled trade between the Roman world and India and patronized the Buddhist caves of western India.

sources.cite: Nasik cave inscriptions of Gautamiputra Satakarni

name: Teotihuacan
summary: A planned city of perhaps 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its influence reached Maya cities such as Tikal in 378 CE.

name: Moche
capital: Huacas del Sol y de la Luna
summary: A society of the north coast of Peru famed for realistic portrait pottery, metalwork and adobe pyramids.

name: Nazca
summary: A culture of Peru's southern desert known for the Nazca Lines geoglyphs and polychrome pottery, successor to the Paracas culture.

sources.cite: Nazca Lines (studied by Maria Reiche from 1946); Cahuachi

name: Chavín
summary: An Andean religious and artistic horizon centred on the temple of Chavín de Huántar, whose style spread across Peru.

sources.cite: Chavín de Huántar, J. C. Tello (1919) and later excavations

name: Zapotec
summary: A people of Oaxaca who built Monte Albán, one of Mesoamerica's first cities, and one of its earliest writing systems.

sources.cite: Monte Albán excavations by Alfonso Caso (1931–1958)

name: Sui dynasty
summary: Reunified China in 589 after nearly four centuries of division and built the Grand Canal, but exhausted itself in wars against Goguryeo.

name: Göktürk Khaganate
summary: The first Turkic empire, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea. It exchanged embassies with Byzantium (568) and allied with Heraclius against Persia.

sources.cite: Orkhon inscriptions (Kul Tigin and Bilge Khagan, 732–735)

name: Avar Khaganate
summary: Steppe horsemen who settled in the Carpathian Basin, extorted tribute from Byzantium and besieged Constantinople with the Persians in 626. Charlemagne's armies broke them in the 790s.

sources.cite: Theodore Synkellos, homily on the siege of 626
Avar cemeteries of the Carpathian Basin

name: Early Slavs
summary: Slavic-speaking groups spread across eastern and central Europe and into the Balkans from the sixth century, settling much of Greece and the Danube provinces.

name: Lombard Kingdom
summary: A Germanic people who invaded Italy three years after Justinian's death, confining Byzantine rule to Ravenna, Rome and the south. Charlemagne conquered their kingdom in 774.

sources.cite: Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards (late 8th c.)

name: Rashidun Caliphate
summary: The first four caliphs after Muhammad. Arab armies conquered Syria, Egypt and the Sasanian Empire in two decades, taking Byzantium's richest provinces.

sources.cite: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings

name: First Bulgarian Empire
summary: Founded when Asparukh's Bulgars defeated Constantine IV south of the Danube. Under Krum and Symeon it repeatedly threatened Constantinople, until Basil II 'the Bulgar-slayer' annexed it in 1018.

sources.cite: Leo the Deacon; John Skylitzes, Synopsis

name: Khazar Khaganate
summary: A Turkic khaganate between the Black Sea and the Caspian, Byzantium's ally against the Arabs. Its ruling elite adopted Judaism. Sviatoslav of Kiev destroyed it around 965–969.

name: Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba
summary: Founded by an Umayyad survivor, Abd al-Rahman I. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III claimed the caliphate, and Córdoba became the largest city in Western Europe before collapsing into taifa kingdoms.

sources.cite: Great Mosque of Córdoba; Madinat al-Zahra

name: Papal States
summary: Territories in central Italy ruled by the popes, founded on Pepin's 'Donation' of former Byzantine lands. Italy annexed Rome in 1870.

name: Norse and Vikings
summary: Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers who reached from Dublin to Baghdad and Newfoundland. As Varangians they founded the Rus' state and served in the Byzantine emperor's guard.

sources.cite: Runestones, e.g. the Greece runestones of Sweden
Birka and Hedeby trading towns; Oseberg ship

name: Tibetan Empire
summary: Unified by Songtsen Gampo, Tibet fought the Tang for Central Asia and briefly occupied Chang'an in 763.

sources.cite: Old Tibetan Annals and Chronicle (Dunhuang manuscripts)

name: Uyghur Khaganate
summary: Successor to the Göktürks on the Mongolian steppe, whose cavalry rescued the Tang during the An Lushan rebellion. The Kyrgyz destroyed it in 840.

name: Pala Empire
summary: Buddhist kings of Bengal and Bihar who patronized the great monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.

name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
summary: A Deccan dynasty that the Arab traveller Sulaiman counted among the world's four great kingdoms. It built the rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora.

name: Great Moravia
summary: The first major Slavic state in Central Europe, where the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius created a Slavonic liturgy and alphabet in 863. The Magyars overran it.

name: Kingdom of Hungary
summary: Magyar tribes settled the Carpathian Basin in 895. Stephen I was crowned Christian king in 1000. The kingdom was a major Balkan power until the Ottomans destroyed its army at Mohács in 1526.

name: Pechenegs
summary: Turkic nomads of the Black Sea steppe whom Byzantium paid to check the Rus' and Bulgars. Alexios I annihilated them at Levounion in 1091.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
summary: An Ismaili Shi'a caliphate that conquered Egypt and founded Cairo, rivalling both the Abbasids and Byzantium. Saladin ended it in 1171.

name: Liao dynasty (Khitan)
summary: A Khitan empire across Mongolia, Manchuria and northern China that extracted tribute from the Song. The Jurchen overthrew it. Its name gave 'Cathay' to European languages.

name: Goryeo (Korea)
summary: The dynasty that gave Korea its name. It reunified the peninsula, printed the Tripitaka Koreana and endured Mongol overlordship.

name: Chola Empire
summary: A Tamil dynasty that conquered Sri Lanka and sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya in 1025. Its bronze sculptures and temples are among India's finest.

sources.cite: Chola copper-plate grants and temple inscriptions

name: Srivijaya
summary: A Malay maritime empire controlling the Strait of Malacca, a centre of Buddhist learning visited by the Chinese pilgrim Yijing.

name: Japan (Yamato to Heian)
summary: From the Yamato court of the great keyhole tombs to the Heian aristocracy of The Tale of Genji. Power passed to warrior clans after the Genpei War of 1180–85.

sources.cite: Murasaki Shikibu, The Tale of Genji (c. 1010)

name: Toltec
summary: A central Mexican state centred on Tula, later idealized by the Aztecs as the source of civilization.

name: Wari Empire
summary: An Andean state with planned administrative centres and roads, a forerunner of Inca statecraft.

sources.cite: Wari site, Ayacucho; El Castillo de Huarmey royal tomb (found 2012)

name: Tiwanaku
summary: A ceremonial city near Lake Titicaca whose stone gateways and raised-field farming supported a wide sphere of influence.

sources.cite: Tiwanaku: Gateway of the Sun and Akapana pyramid

name: Chimú
summary: Coastal Peruvian kingdom whose capital Chan Chan was the largest adobe city in the Americas. The Inca conquered it around 1470.

sources.cite: Spanish colonial accounts of Chimú dynastic lists

name: Mississippian culture (Cahokia)
summary: Maize-farming chiefdoms of the American Midwest and Southeast. Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico around 1100, with the vast earthwork of Monks Mound.

name: Ancestral Puebloans
summary: Builders of the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde. Severe drought helped drive migrations south around 1300.

sources.cite: Tree-ring dating of Mesa Verde cliff dwellings

name: Kanem–Bornu
summary: A Sahelian empire around Lake Chad ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty for about a thousand years, a key hub of trans-Saharan trade.

sources.cite: Ahmad Furtu, chronicle of Mai Idris Alooma (1570s)

name: Makuria (Christian Nubia)
summary: A Christian Nubian kingdom that defeated Arab invaders in 652 and signed the long-lasting Baqt treaty with Egypt.

sources.cite: Old Dongola and Faras cathedral paintings (Polish excavations)

name: Ethiopian Empire
capital: Mobile royal camp, later Gondar and Addis Ababa
summary: The Solomonic dynasty claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Its emperors ruled the Christian highlands for seven centuries.

sources.cite: Royal chronicles of the Solomonic emperors

name: Great Zimbabwe
summary: A Shona state whose capital's dry-stone enclosures held perhaps 18,000 people, wealthy from gold exports to the Swahili coast.

sources.cite: Great Zimbabwe ruins (UNESCO); Persian and Chinese ceramics found on site

name: Swahili city-states
summary: Muslim trading towns of the East African coast linking African gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean world.

sources.cite: Great Mosque and Husuni Kubwa, Kilwa Kisiwani

name: Kingdom of Benin
summary: A West African kingdom famous for its brass plaques and walled capital. A British punitive expedition sacked it in 1897 and looted the Benin Bronzes.

sources.cite: Portuguese accounts from 1485; Dapper, Description of Africa (1668)

name: Kingdom of Kongo
summary: A central African kingdom whose king Afonso I (1509–1543) adopted Christianity and corresponded with Portugal and the Pope. The slave trade and civil war weakened it.

sources.cite: Letters of Afonso I to João III of Portugal (1526)

name: Oyo Empire
summary: A Yoruba cavalry empire of the savanna that dominated the region of modern south-western Nigeria and Benin in the 17th–18th centuries.

sources.cite: Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (1897, from oral tradition)

name: Ghaznavid Empire
summary: A Turkic dynasty whose sultan Mahmud raided deep into India. Its court sheltered the scholar al-Biruni and the poet Ferdowsi.

name: Seljuk Turks
capital: Nishapur, Isfahan; Konya for the Sultanate of Rum
summary: Oghuz Turks who took Baghdad in 1055 and broke Byzantine Anatolia at Manzikert in 1071. A branch founded the Sultanate of Rum at Konya, which dominated central Anatolia until Mongol conquest.

sources.cite: Ibn Bibi, history of the Rum Seljuks
Alaeddin Mosque and caravanserais of Anatolia

name: Normans in southern Italy and Sicily
summary: Norman adventurers took Byzantine Apulia (Bari fell in 1071) and Arab Sicily, then invaded the Byzantine Balkans under Robert Guiscard. Roger II made Sicily a kingdom in 1130.

sources.cite: William of Apulia, Deeds of Robert Guiscard

name: Cumans (Kipchaks)
summary: Turkic nomads who replaced the Pechenegs on the western steppe, fought and allied with Byzantium, Rus' and Hungary, and helped found the Second Bulgarian Empire. The Mongols scattered them.

sources.cite: Rus' Primary Chronicle; Tale of Igor's Campaign

name: Republic of Venice
summary: A lagoon city that began as a Byzantine dependency and became a maritime empire. Byzantium's 1082 trade privileges enriched it, and its fleet steered the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople. Napoleon ended it in 1797.

sources.cite: Chrysobull of Alexios I for Venice (1082)
Geoffrey of Villehardouin, Conquest of Constantinople
Basilica of San Marco and the looted Horses of St Mark

name: Republic of Genoa
summary: Venice's great commercial rival, which won privileges from Michael VIII in 1261 and held Galata across the Golden Horn and Caffa in Crimea.

name: Crusader states
summary: Kingdoms and counties founded by the First Crusade at Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli and Jerusalem. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187; the Mamluks took Acre, the last stronghold, in 1291.

sources.cite: William of Tyre, History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea
Krak des Chevaliers; Acre crusader city

name: Kingdom of Georgia
summary: United under the Bagrationi dynasty, Georgia peaked under David IV the Builder and Queen Tamar, who helped found the Empire of Trebizond in 1204.

name: Armenian kingdoms
capital: Artaxata, Ani, later Sis in Cilicia
summary: Armenia was a buffer contested by Rome and Persia and in 301 became the first state to adopt Christianity. The Bagratid kingdom fell to Byzantium in 1045, and the Cilician kingdom to the Mamluks in 1375. Several Byzantine emperors were of Armenian descent.

sources.cite: Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians

name: Second Bulgarian Empire
summary: Founded when the brothers Peter and Asen revolted against Isaac II Angelos. Kaloyan captured the Latin emperor Baldwin I at Adrianople in 1205. It fell to the Ottomans in 1393–96.

sources.cite: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, Conquest of Constantinople

name: Medieval Serbia
summary: Under the Nemanjić dynasty Serbia grew from a Byzantine vassal into the dominant Balkan power. Stefan Dušan was crowned 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks' in 1346. The Ottomans annexed the last Serbian despotate in 1459.

sources.cite: Lives of Serbian kings by Archbishop Danilo II

name: Latin Empire
summary: The crusader state set up after the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, ruled by Flemish and French nobles, with Venice controlling much of the Aegean. Nicaea recaptured the city in 1261.

sources.cite: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, Conquest of Constantinople
Robert de Clari, Conquest of Constantinople

name: Empire of Nicaea
summary: The most successful Byzantine successor state after 1204, built by Theodore I Laskaris and John III Vatatzes. Michael VIII Palaiologos retook Constantinople in 1261.

name: Empire of Trebizond
summary: Founded by the Komnenos grandsons of Andronikos I with Georgian help. It outlasted Constantinople by eight years before surrendering to Mehmed II in 1461.

name: Despotate of Epirus
summary: A Byzantine successor state in western Greece. Under Theodore Komnenos Doukas it took Thessalonica in 1224 and rivalled Nicaea, until defeat by Bulgaria at Klokotnitsa in 1230.

name: Ayyubid Sultanate
summary: Founded by Saladin, who ended the Fatimid caliphate, defeated the crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem in 1187. Its Mamluk soldiers overthrew the dynasty in Egypt in 1250.

sources.cite: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, Life of Saladin

name: Mamluk Sultanate
summary: A regime of slave-soldiers that stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut and expelled the last crusaders. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516–17.

name: Golden Horde
summary: The north-western khanate of the Mongol Empire, overlord of the Rus' principalities and a trading partner of Byzantium, Genoa and Mamluk Egypt.

name: Timurid Empire
summary: Timur's conquests devastated Persia, Syria and India. His victory at Ankara in 1402 nearly destroyed the Ottomans and bought Byzantium half a century. His heirs presided over a Persianate cultural flowering.

sources.cite: Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane

name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
summary: Europe's last pagan state became, after union with Poland, one of the largest states in Europe, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea.

name: Kingdom of Poland
summary: From Mieszko I's baptism in 966 to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Partitioned out of existence by Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1795.

name: Teutonic Order state
summary: A crusading order that conquered the pagan Prussians and ruled the southern Baltic. It was defeated at Grunwald in 1410 and secularized as the Duchy of Prussia in 1525.

sources.cite: Peter of Dusburg, Chronicle of the Prussian Land

name: Novgorod Republic
summary: A merchant republic of northern Rus' with an elected prince, trading with the Hanseatic League. Ivan III annexed it to Muscovy in 1478.

name: Kingdom of France
summary: From Hugh Capet's election to the monarchy's fall in the Revolution. French crusaders led the Fourth Crusade, and French dynasties ruled Latin Constantinople and Achaea.

name: Crown of Castile
summary: The leading kingdom of the Christian reconquest of Iberia. With Aragon it formed the core of the Spanish monarchy after the marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand.

name: Almoravid and Almohad empires
summary: Two successive Berber religious-reform empires that ruled the Maghreb and al-Andalus, halting the Christian advance in Iberia for a century and a half.

name: Khwarazmian Empire
summary: A Central Asian power whose shah provoked Chinggis Khan by killing his envoys in 1218, bringing the Mongol storm to the Islamic world.

sources.cite: Ata-Malik Juvayni, History of the World Conqueror

name: Western Xia
summary: A Tangut state on the Silk Road with its own script, destroyed by Chinggis Khan in 1227.

name: Jin dynasty (Jurchen)
summary: Jurchen conquerors who destroyed the Liao and took northern China from the Song in 1127. The Mongols ended it in 1234.

name: Champa
summary: Cham kingdoms on the coast of central Vietnam, rivals of the Khmer and Đại Việt, known for brick temples such as My Son.

sources.cite: Cham inscriptions in Sanskrit and Old Cham

name: Đại Việt
summary: The independent Vietnamese state from Ngô Quyền's victory at Bạch Đằng in 938 onward. It repelled three Mongol invasions and expanded south at Champa's expense.

sources.cite: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)

name: Pagan Kingdom
summary: The first Burmese empire, which filled the plain of Bagan with more than 2,000 surviving Buddhist temples.

name: Majapahit
summary: A Javanese thalassocracy that claimed overlordship of much of the Indonesian archipelago under the minister Gajah Mada.

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
summary: A Siamese kingdom that sacked Angkor in 1431 and became a cosmopolitan trading hub, until Burmese armies destroyed its capital in 1767.

name: Vijayanagara Empire
summary: A south Indian Hindu empire whose capital at Hampi astonished Persian and Portuguese visitors. It was defeated at Talikota in 1565.

name: Mixtec kingdoms
summary: City-kingdoms of Oaxaca whose screenfold codices record genealogies, such as that of the 11th-century ruler Eight Deer Jaguar Claw.
